units.translation: where Reisig conjectured ἀντόνειρον [instead of a dream], whose gloss may be ἰσόνειρον [like a dream], just as ἀντίμοιρον [instead of fate] is explained by ἰσόμοιρον [like fate], about which we have just spoken.
It is not found elsewhere, except in one passage of Philo vol. 2 p. 495. 13 τίς δὲ τοῖς πρώτοις γενομένοις ἰσόπαις ἣν οἰκειότης [what kinship was there, equal to a child, with the first beings?]
what kinship was there, equal to a child, with the first beings?
This word too is not found elsewhere.
young marrow – equal to an old man
weighing the scales with unequal fortune
The first syllable, as often in epic poets, lengthened

unless οἷον [such as] should be written. In Herodian περὶ μον. λέξ. [on monosyllabic words] p. 36, 20 is read ἴσον ἐν οὐρανῷ [equal in heaven]: but èv is rightly omitted in other grammarians indicated in the notes.

The adjectives ἰσόμοιρος [sharing equally] and ἰσόνειρος [like a dream] are uncertain with the first syllable lengthened, about which we spoke above. But ἰσόθεος ι [godlike] is correctly long in the dactylic meters Pers. 80 856, and ἴσου [equal] which I restored at Ag. 122 ἰδὼν δύο λήμασιν ἴσους | Ἀτρεΐδας [seeing the two Atreidae equal in spirit] for λήμασι δισσούς [with twofold spirits].
neither less nor equal, being left behind
so as to obtain an equal share
light equal to the eyes of the gods
how shall I accomplish it by saying an equal thing?
for the number of the lots is equal
if I had a cloak equal to the sky
and of the ever-flourishing in leaves, equal to the golden olive
seeing the two Atreidae equal in spirit
having an equal number of votes
having an equal number of votes
Orestes wins, even if he is judged with an equal number of votes
the judgment came out with equal votes
Another example of this word is in Anna Comnena 13 p. 387c. and of the adverb ἰσοψύχως [with equal spirit] in Eustathius p. 831, 52.
and you strengthen for me the power equal in spirit, heart-biting, from women
to set, to raise. Of raising a cry
to set, to raise. Of raising a cry
The perfect ἕστηκα [I stand] (Doric ἕστακα) and the aorist ἔστην [I stood] have the meaning of standing.
Similar examples from Sophocles and Euripides are cited in Thes. vol. 4 p. 692.

where Linwood's conjecture κτίσητε [you may found] is not improbable, a verb which Aeschylus often used in this way, although στήσητε [you may set] could also be said, with which Hermann compared Sophocles OC. 1041 πρὶν ἄν σε τῶν σῶν κύριον στήσω τέκνων [before I set you as master of your children].
what cry are you raising in the house?
nor, goddesses, set the land too grievously troubled for mortals
it stands toward the western regions
and he set up a trophy of Ruin at the gates
the sheep already stand for the slaughter of fire
unless some god stood in the way with his spear
and the upright lock of hair stands on end
